<pre style='white-space:pre-wrap;width:81ex'>feat(sheets): accept the parameter spellings two reflow windows say callers write (#2710)

* feat(sheets): accept the parameter spellings the 09-04..07 reflow rejected

The 09-04..07 reflow attributes 343031 failures across the sheets domain, and
the four largest clusters that survive on HEAD all carry well-formed intent in
a spelling the flag refuses while its own error text names the fix.

border_type is the largest single style field at 46035 rejections. It stayed a
prescription because the field carries two vocabularies -- the Lark OpenAPI's
side selector (FULL_BORDER / OUTER_BORDER) and the CSS-ish line word every
model reaches for -- and the pair reads as ambiguous from the field name. It
is decidable from the VALUE, and the reading that blocked it was backwards:
set_cell_range applies each side to every cell of the range, verified on a
live sheet (border_styles.top over A1:C3 leaves a top border on all nine
cells), so FULL_BORDER is exactly border_styles.all. What genuinely has no
expression here is the subset values -- OUTER_BORDER, INNER_BORDER and the two
axis words -- which now prescribe the subset they mean instead of a field list.
border_width (919) folds onto weight, border_all (242) joins the side loop, and
the one-value shorthand every external vocabulary has (border:"solid",
border:2 -- 5903) is read rather than answered with "must be an object".

--writes rejected a top-level sheet selector outright, on the reasoning that
one selector per item leaves no precedence table to remember; the precedence
worth remembering is the one the caller wrote, and every single-sheet payload
had to repeat it per item to say nothing new (19059). It now fills in for the
items that name no sheet, as --allow-overwrite already does, and an item's own
selector -- including one spelled in a sheet-prefixed range -- still wins.

A missing required flag answered with cobra's bare "required flag(s) X not
set" (20447) now keeps those words and gains what the flag takes plus the
command's own example, so the retry needs no --help round trip.
+cond-format-create additionally stops demanding --ranges / --rule-type from a
caller who wrote the whole rule in --properties: the payload's schema requires
both at its root, so it has them, and its message names the exact path when it
does not.

Three smaller ones on the same contract: short --cells rows are padded with {}
(3063), which is the fix the rejection spelled out word for word; the openpyxl
and xlsxwriter font flags (bold, italic, underline, font_name -- 2192) put the
concept in the key and the on/off in the value, so each carries its own value
reading and an unreadable one keeps its prescription; and the dimension enums
take the plural and the abbreviation (2898).

* feat(sheets): size a --cells write from its payload, and stop rejecting table shapes a sheet allows

+cells-set enforced that --range and --cells agree, in one direction only: a
payload smaller than the stated range was narrowed to it, a larger one was
rejected. That was the least defensible of the three available positions. The
command overwrites non-empty cells by default (--allow-overwrite), a bare
single-cell range has always been an anchor, and every library these callers
arrive from sizes a write from its data (gspread's update("A1", values),
openpyxl's anchor assignment). The range is now read for its top-left and the
extent follows the payload in both directions; --start-cell answers as an alias
so the anchor can be spelled the way +csv-put already spells it.

What this costs is a real check: a payload built one row short now writes
quietly where it used to fail here. So the note fitCellsRange already produced
for narrowing is now produced for both directions and says which way it moved
and what shipped. A range whose sheet prefix disagrees with --sheet-name used
to be caught sideways, by the extent check failing on a range that was never
sized; it gets its own message now.

The table payload stops rejecting three shapes a sheet allows. A repeated
column heading is what the source data looked like, not a mistake -- dtypes and
formats are keyed by name, so an entry for a repeated name applies to each of
its columns, the same reading the caller would get by spelling it twice (1334).
A dtypes or formats key that differs from its column only in spacing or casing
folds onto it when exactly one column answers, since both the key and the
header usually come from the same source data and only one of them picked up
the stray space (657); a key no column answers to under any spelling still
reports as unknown rather than being dropped. And a NEW workbook names the
sub-sheets the caller left unnamed, in payload order, skipping any name they
did spell, which is the SheetN series the workbook would have had anyway (1564
across both entry points). +table-put keeps that rejection: there the name
selects the sub-sheet and creates what is absent, so an invented one would
write somewhere nobody picked. Its message now points at the sheet list.

Counts are 09-04..07 rejections; the --cells extent accounted for 21425 across
both directions.

* feat(sheets): fold flag spellings, and name the sibling a flag belongs to

The unknown-flag cluster is the domain's third largest (31277 rejections over
09-04..07) and the one the reflow cannot itemize: the pipeline masks quoted
values, and a flag name arrives quoted, so every spelling merges into one
fingerprint. Two of its shapes are answerable without knowing a single name.

A spelling that differs from a real flag only in separators or casing is one
name, not a new one. --sheetName is what a caller reading the JSON side of the
API writes, --sheet_Name is that habit half-corrected, --sheet.name is the
JSON-path one; the underscore form was already folded, which left the rule
stated but not finished. It is now one index over the names each command
answers to, keyed by letters and digits alone, so the fold costs no per-name
entry -- and it only ever resolves onto a flag that exists, which is what keeps
it from renaming a caller's genuine mistake into something they did not ask
for. A name no flag answers to still reaches the unknown-flag error with its
did-you-mean intact.

The other shape is a flag that exists, on a different command. --csv on
+cells-set, --font-color on +cells-set, --widths on +rows-resize: the caller
reached for a real capability and knocked on the wrong door, and the answer is
which door, not a list of what is behind this one. That is a fact about the
surface rather than a guess, so it outranks an edit-distance neighbour -- but
only when the neighbour is not a near-typo, or --range on a command spelling it
--ranges would get a tour of the domain instead of the rename it needs. The
near-typo budget is two edits and no more than half the name, which is what
stops --csv from reading as a misspelling of --as.

* feat(sheets): read a payload written in another JSON convention

A payload flag takes strict JSON, and 12746 of the 09-04..07 rejections are a
payload encoding/json could not read. The position each one failed at says
which convention it arrived in, and the shapes split cleanly in two.

A bare CJK run where a value belongs accounts for 4939 of them. Nothing is
wrong with the encoding there, whatever the message looks like: the parser
reports the run's first BYTE, and CJK leads with 0xE4..0xE9, which prints as
ä / å / æ. The quotes around the string are simply missing. Python's literals
and single quotes, a trailing comma, and an unquoted object key make up most of
the rest. Each of those is the caller's own data in the spelling of whatever
produced it, with one reading, so they are now rewritten on a fallback parse
and the payload goes through.

The other half is refused, deliberately. A bracket that does not match (3602)
and a payload cut short (1222) can only be repaired by guessing where the
caller's data ended, and a guess that lands writes a wrong table in silence
instead of failing where the caller can see it. A digit-led run is refused for
the same reason: "123中文" is equally one string that lost its quotes and two
cells that lost their comma. When the repair declines, the error still
describes the payload as written, not the attempt.

The repair never runs on input encoding/json accepted, never touches the text
inside a string that is quoted, and must itself parse strictly or it is
discarded. It is wired at the three places a payload decodes: parseJSONFlag for
--cells / --writes / --styles and their siblings, and the two flags that decode
into their own wire structs (--sheets, whose 5072 rejections are the largest
share of any single flag, and --values).

* feat(sheets): resolve a missing sheet selector against the workbook

"specify at least one of --sheet-id or --sheet-name" is 11115 rejections over
09-04..07, and eval traces show every one of them recovering on the next call.
That says the gap was never that a selector is needed. It was which name to
pass, and the workbook is the thing that knows: a freshly created one has a
single sheet, and every other one answers a lookup the caller was about to run
by hand anyway.

The execute path now asks. One sheet is the sheet meant, so it is filled in;
several are listed by name in the error, which is the one shot the caller
needed. The lookup costs a request and only on the path that was going to fail.

Getting there moved where the requirement is settled. resolveSheetSelector
enforced "exactly one" the moment a flag was read, which is Validate — offline,
and long before anything could look a sheet up. It now settles only the mutual
exclusion, and the requirement itself belongs to the execute path
(resolveSheetSelectorExec) or, for the builders that check it themselves, to
requireSheetSelector as before. Two places keep the old rejection deliberately:
--dry-run, which sends nothing and so cannot resolve either, and would
otherwise print a request whose selector the CLI would have filled in; and a
+batch-update sub-op, whose contract is that each op names its own sheet.

* feat(sheets): read the payload vocabulary the remaining rejections arrived in

Four clusters left in the 09-04..07 reflow whose payloads name things this
domain already carries, under the vocabulary the caller came with. Each fold
below is decided by what the value IS, never by the key alone, so a key that
means something else here keeps its meaning.

--properties on the cond-format pair. A comparison arrives under `operator`
(the OpenAPI's name), `criteria` (Excel's), `comparison`, `compare` or
`condition`, and the entry carrying it is otherwise complete; 2852 rejections
said compare_type was missing. Only a value the compare enum recognizes moves,
which is what keeps timePeriod's own `operator` — whose "is" is also a compare
word — where it belongs, alongside the shape-key guard that was already there.
The `font` slot is one string here ("bold", "italic", "bold italic") while
every font vocabulary spells the two effects as flags or as a list, in no fixed
order: 972 rejections were the object form alone. Recognized effects are now
collected and re-emitted in the enum's order; an unrecognized one is left for
the schema.

--styles items (3938). The sheet selector is `name` here and sheet_name
everywhere else in this domain; a section is spelled by its effect
(row_heights, column_widths, merges) as often as by its name, and in the
singular as often as the plural. Three of these the distance ranker could
already name, which means the error spelled the fix and declined to apply it. A
section written as one object lifts into its one-entry list, and the bare item
list needs no envelope, which --sheets has accepted since the 08-29..31 round.

Column objects (2559). An object column entry carries its heading under
`title`, `header`, `label`, `column`, `field` or `key` when it does not spell
it `name`. The key is consumed once read, so the vocabulary check downstream
does not then report it as one the entry has no room for.

--cells given one dimension (796). A flat list is a row in every library these
callers arrive from, and a lone scalar is the one cell it names. The exception
is the caller's own range: one column wide and several rows tall can only be
asking for a column, and a row there would write where they did not point. A
mixed payload covers neither reading and still fails.

Payload normalizers now take the flagView, which is what lets the flat-list
lift consult the range at all; the rest ignore it.

* feat(sheets): fit the declared columns to the rows that arrived

Two of the table-shape rejections read as ambiguous and are not, once the
result is what decides rather than the payload.

A row longer than `columns` (2779) first has its trailing EMPTY cells dropped:
a nil or a blank string past the last column writes nothing, so the row was
already the width it declared and the padding came from whatever generated it.
What is still longer gets the columns it needs with BLANK headings, which is
the shape a table with unnamed trailing columns has and one this payload
already accepts on the way in. Naming them would put a word in the caller's
header row that they never wrote; dropping the values would lose data.

A sheet that declares no columns but carries rows (2299) is the --values shape
spelled on --sheets, so it takes the --values treatment: positional type-less
columns and no header row, which writes exactly the block that arrived and
nothing above it. A caller who asked for a header row explicitly keeps the
rejection — there is no telling what they wanted it to say.

The shapes the loose-JSON repair refuses now say WHERE. A bracket that does not
match and a payload cut short can only be fixed by the caller, and "invalid
character '}' after array element" does not locate it in an 8 KB body. Go
carries the offset on the syntax error and leaves it out of the text; the hint
puts it back with the run either side of it, on all three payload parse paths.

* feat(sheets): close a whole-column style range against the sheet's own grid

A cell style takes a rectangle, because the CLI builds the cell matrix itself
and a matrix needs both extents. "A:C" and "3:5" carry only one, so they were
rejected at parse time (1208 rejections under --styles over 09-04..07) — but
the missing extent is not a guess, it is the sheet's own row or column count,
and the execute path can read it.

It does, once per invocation and only when a range needs it, off the same
workbook-structure call the sheet selector already learned to make. "A:C" on a
200-row sheet is A1:C200; an oversized result then meets the same stamp budget
an explicit range of that size would, which is the honest answer rather than a
silent half-write.

Only cell_styles ranges are closed. row_sizes and col_sizes take a dimension
range by design ("2:10", "A:C"), and bounding those would turn their own
vocabulary into an error.

Pre-flight cannot read a grid, so it stands in a rectangle that keeps the axis
the caller did state (A:C becomes A1:C1) and checks everything else about the
item as usual; the real extent is settled on the execute path. --dry-run keeps
the rejection, since it sends nothing and cannot resolve the range either.

* feat(sheets): take the flag names the backflow says callers actually write

The full-window flag table (doubao backflow, 09-01..08, 72801 rows carrying an
unknown flag) settles what the reflow could only guess at: the names are all
there, per command, with counts. Probing every one of the top 75 against HEAD
splits them four ways — 17154 rows already alias silently, 33932 already draw a
curated prescription, 4365 now name the sibling that owns the flag, and 7901
get nothing but a did-you-mean. That last set is this change.

Most of it is one shape: the surface spells a locator in full and the caller
reaches for the short form. --sheet for --sheet-name is 765 rows across 21
commands, --spreadsheet 541 across 17, --ranges 525 across 18, the output
family 450 across 19. Per-command entries would be 70-odd rows of table for
one idea, so these move to a domain table applied wherever the canonical flag
exists and the alias does not — which also keeps +cond-format-create's real
--ranges, and lets +cells-unmerge keep its own answer for --ranges, since there
the caller is asking for several spans and the fix is how to send several.

Three more are renames whose value changes shape on the way, and each already
had the reader it needed. A bare A1 range becomes the one-element list --ranges
takes (1862 rows on cond-format alone). A bare line word becomes all four sides
of --border-styles, so --border-type solid, --border thin and --border 2 carry
(1491) — and a bare --border-styles solid now works for the same reason. A lone
scalar becomes the one cell --cells takes, which is what --value means (167).

The rest prescribe, because the value belongs somewhere else: the index
vocabulary against a CLI that names dimensions by A1 span (579), a rule
parameter that belongs inside --properties (537), an --include category spelled
as its own flag (309), a remote image URL where a local file is uploaded (74).
And the border family's per-side, per-attribute tail gets a prefix rule rather
than an entry each: --border-bottom-color and its kind all have the same answer.

* feat(sheets): finish the flag-name tail, and stop rejecting a defensive --yes

The long tail of the backflow's flag table is the same two shapes as its head,
one command at a time. Renames whose value carries unchanged join the tables:
the search text (--query, --search), the fill colour (--back-color, --bg-color,
--fill-color), the CSV body (--csv-data, --text), the dropdown list (--items),
the rename target (--new-sheet-name), the sort spec (--sort-spec). Two
prescriptions that these now shadow are deleted rather than left to rot.

Prescriptions cover what moves: the index vocabulary on the two dimension
commands the earlier pass missed, and a formula rule, whose formula belongs in
--properties under rule_type "expression".

--yes is a different thing. The framework registers it on high-risk writes and
reads it only there, so a caller who passes it everywhere — 437 rows over 14
commands — is saying "do not stop to ask" to a command that never asks. That
request is already honoured; refusing the flag fails a call that is otherwise
complete. It is accepted and ignored where it means nothing, hidden from
--help so the flag is still taught only where it decides something.

Measured over the 275 (command, flag) pairs that carry 97% of the domain's
unknown-flag rows, by probing each against the binary before and after: rows
that now parse silently go 29.0% -> 36.8%, rows answered by a curated
prescription 50.6% -> 52.4%, and rows left with nothing but a did-you-mean
11.8% -> 2.7%.

* fix(sheets): address the review findings on the tolerance layer

The panic first. fitColumnsToRows widens the column list after padShortRows has
already run, and both the validator and the writer index a row by column
position, so a ragged payload — `data:[[1,2],[3]]`, with or without declared
columns — indexed past the short row and took the process down. Both paths
re-pad against the count they settled on.

Ordering defects of the same kind, each found by the review:

- wrapBareListValue ran after the loose-JSON repair, which turns a token with
  no punctuation into a valid JSON string, so `--ranges Sheet1!A1` reached the
  array check as a scalar. The wrap goes first.
- normalizeCondFormatFontValue ran after the flat-word loop, which reads
  style["font"] as a string; an object there read as empty and the flat word
  replaced it, so `{"font":{"bold":true},"italic":true}` lost bold.
- A border_type side selector wrote `solid` onto its side while the attributes
  the caller spelled out had already folded onto `all`, leaving a dashed box
  with a solid left edge where one dashed left border was asked for. The
  selection now carries those attributes with it.

Failures that were being swallowed or misreported. A workbook-structure read
that fails on authentication, permission or transport was reported as "specify
at least one of --sheet-id or --sheet-name" by the selector resolver and as
"unsupported range form" by the style bounder; both now return what actually
failed. A sheet-prefixed whole-column range ("Summary!A:C") never matched the
bounder's patterns and was rejected as unsupported.

Rewrites that could pick a winner at random, or drop what they could not read.
Two stray dtypes keys folding onto one column, and positional dtypes over a
repeated heading, both resolved by map order; both now refuse. A font object
carrying an effect this enum has no room for (underline) had that effect
dropped in silence; it is left for the schema. A single-quoted string carrying
`\n` was repaired into a literal backslash and n, rewriting the caller's data;
the escapes JSON, Python and JavaScript agree on are decoded and anything else
leaves the payload unrepaired.

Resource and protocol. Squaring off one very wide row over many short ones
allocated the rectangle before any validator could refuse it, so the cap is
checked against the padded size first. --values probed json.Valid before
decoding, scanning and copying every payload twice on the path that needs no
repair. +sheet-delete no longer resolves "the only sheet": deleting a sub-sheet
takes the whole thing with it and has no narrower target to state.

Reach. The deferred-selector change only took effect where Validate ran through
validateViaInput; the object-CRUD factories and the three chart commands
validate through their own callbacks and still rejected an omitted selector
before Execute could resolve it. The squashed flag fold returned the canonical
name without staging alias provenance, so --csvFile reached --csv as inline
text rather than a path.

Smaller ones: every missing required flag now survives in Params rather than
only the last in the scalar Param; usage text and the JSON syntax window
truncate on rune boundaries; the --styles root error names the bare list it now
accepts; the trailing-comma trim truncates its buffer instead of rebuilding the
prefix once per level; liftFlatCellsRow no longer trips asasalint. Three test
assertions that could not observe what they pinned were tightened.

* fix(sheets): answer the deferred selector on object-create, and merge into an existing side

Two findings from the re-review, both of them consequences of the previous
round rather than of the branch's original shape.

Deferring the missing selector in Validate only helps if execution answers it.
The object-create factory reads its selector from flags the spec names itself
(createSheetIDFlag / createSheetNameFlag), so it cannot go through
resolveSheetSelectorExec, and it was still passing the empty pair straight to
the input builder — which moved the same failure one layer deeper instead of
resolving it. The workbook lookup is split out so both readers share it, and
the create path calls it with whatever pair its own flags produced.

The border side selection replaced the selected side's map with the attributes
folded onto "all". A caller who spelled an attribute for that side alone
(border_left_color) had it dropped, because the narrower statement was
overwritten by the broader one. Only the attributes the side lacks are copied
now.

TestObjectCreate_RequiresSheetSelector moves to --dry-run, which is where the
rejection still belongs: a preview sends nothing, so it cannot resolve the
sheet either.

* test(sheets): pin the sheet-prefix conflict by the message it now carries

The dry-run E2E case for a prefixed --range beside a contradicting selector
asserted the cells-vs-range mismatch, which is how that conflict used to
surface: the range was never sized, so the extent check failed on it. The
conflict has its own message now (checkRangeSheetAgreesWithSelector), and it
names both sheets, so the case pins that instead — through the escaping the
JSON envelope puts on the message's own quotes.

The command still exits 2 on the same input; only what it says changed.

* chore(sheets): sync skill artifacts from spec, and keep --start-cell anchoring

Regenerates flag_defs_gen.go / flag_schemas_gen.go from the synced
data/*.json, so the compiled defs stop disagreeing with their source.

The sync declares --start-cell as a hidden flag of +cells-set. The
normalizer short-circuits on registered flags before it consults
perCommandFlagAliases, so the alias that used to carry that spelling over
to --range became unreachable the moment the flag existed -- silently, with
no conflict error, turning a working call into "--range is required".
cellsSetInputWithNote now reads the flag directly and --range stays
canonical when both are given, which is also what the alias table entry
was there for; the entry itself is dropped as dead.

* feat(sheets): take the parameter spellings the 09-08..12 catalog rejected

Replayed the window's top templates against this branch first: roughly half
of the sheets parameter rejections are already answered here and only await a
release. What follows is what survived that replay.

Renames and placements, each the same input under another spelling:

  - +dim-delete --position reaches --range. +dim-insert carries a real
    --position, so the habit crosses to its sibling; --range takes a lone "5"
    as the single row, which is the only thing "delete at position 5" can
    mean. Kept to --position alone -- --start-index / --end-index name a
    half-open pair whose end would have to be guessed, and this command
    deletes, so a guess is unrecoverable.
  - cell style "wrap" is word_wrap and "text_color" is font_color. wrap_text,
    text_wrap and wrap_strategy were already taken; refusing only the shortest
    of four spellings of one concept is a rule no caller can infer.
  - cond-format compare_type takes the bare comparative (greater, less, above,
    below). gt / ge / >= already resolved.
  - cells[][].cell_styles.border_styles is lifted to its sibling, and a
    border_styles on a styles ITEM moves onto its one cell_styles entry. Both
    errors already named the correct position and then declined to act on it.
    Two borders for one cell, or two candidate ranges, still fail.

A dropdown --options that arrives bare becomes the one-element list it can
only be. Unlike the range flags it does NOT split on commas: an option is a
label the caller wrote, and "Yes, with conditions" is one of them. A comma
list instead gets the split spelled out in the hint to confirm.

Multi-area ranges are answered per command. get_cell_ranges already takes a
LIST, so +cells-get / +dropdown-get / +cond-format-result-get forward the
areas as the several ranges they name. Write and style commands keep the
prescription: fanning one call into several changes what a partial failure
leaves behind.

Two defects found while doing the above, neither in the catalog as such:

  - The multi-area guard read --range through pflag, which normalizes, so on
    a command where --range is an ALIAS it judged the flag being aliased.
    +chart-create-basic is exactly that: it has no real --range, and its
    --data-range is documented to take a comma-separated multi-range. The
    guard had been refusing a supported feature.
  - Only the first area's sheet qualifier was stripped, so an expanded range
    shipped later areas still carrying a prefix beside a sheet_name saying
    the same thing. The qualifier is now lifted once across all areas, which
    requires them to agree; areas naming two sheets are left untouched rather
    than silently retargeted. Splitting respects quotes, since a quoted sheet
    name may itself contain a comma.

* feat(sheets): take the flag names the unknown-flag table says callers write

The per-flag breakdown resolves what the catalog could not: its unknown-flag
bucket normalizes to one row, and +dim-delete --position was only its FIRST
value, not its 92k. The real figure is 19,235. Replaying every (command, flag)
pair over 100 hits showed 65% of that volume was already answered here; these
are renames from what was left.

  - +cells-set-style / +cells-batch-set-style take wrap-text, wrap-strategy,
    text-wrap and bare wrap as --word-wrap. These carried a prescription whose
    stated reason was that the VALUES differ too. They no longer do: the enum
    normalizer already reads true/false, the Google Sheets API words
    (WRAP / OVERFLOW / CLIP) and the bare ones onto this enum, so the name was
    all that was left to change. Values it still refuses (1, yes) fail exactly
    as before, with the enum listed.
  - --border-style joins --border-type / --border / --border-all: a bare line
    word is read as all four sides.
  - +dim-freeze takes the frozen-* and *-count spellings as --rows / --cols.
    Same integer, and the prescription spelled the rename and nothing else.
  - +workbook-export --type joins --file-format / --file-type; the only type
    this command has is the export format.

Deliberately left with their prescriptions: --bold / --font-bold (the value
would have to be translated to an enum, not just the name), the per-side
border flags (they compose INTO the composite flag rather than rename onto
it), and --dimension on the dimension commands (inferred from --range).

Accepted volume over the replayed pairs goes 65% -> 79%.

* fix(sheets): tell the --ranges commands' callers where the sheet goes

A top-level --sheet-name on +cells-batch-clear / +dropdown-delete /
+dropdown-update fell through to the generic locator, which answers with the
OTHER commands the flag is valid on ("--sheet-name is a flag of +cells-clear /
+cells-get / +cells-merge") and never states where the sheet goes here. It
goes in each --ranges entry, as a bare A1 prefix.

--sheet-id gets its own wording rather than the same sentence: a prefix is the
sheet's display name and never a reference_id, so pointing at the prefix form
would be pointing at something that does not exist for that input. It sends
the caller to +sheet-list to trade the id for the name.

The flags stay unknown. Accepting them would make a top-level selector a
second way to say what the payload already says, on commands where the
entries may name different sheets -- and for --sheet-id there is no prefix to
translate it into. The sibling case that DID get accepted (+cells-set
--writes) differs in that --sheet-name was already a flag of that command.

Leaves +table-put / +styles-put alone: their errors already name the field and
show the JSON, which is the whole fix, and `name` is still required there, so
nothing is silently retargeted.

* fix(sheets): let every command that resolves a sheet also defer asking for one

Review found the selector deferral half-wired. The requirement is easy to
satisfy in Execute and easy to miss in Validate, because the two read the
selector from different places: Execute passes the RESOLVED pair into the
input builder, Validate passes the raw flags. A builder calling
requireSheetSelector therefore passes for one caller and fails for the other,
with nothing tying them together.

Sweeping every command whose Execute calls resolveSheetSelectorExec found nine
still rejecting in pre-flight -- more than the review named: +cells-merge,
+cells-unmerge, +rows-resize, +cols-resize, +range-copy, +range-move,
+dim-delete (both --range and --ranges), +dim-hide / +dim-unhide,
+dim-group / +dim-ungroup, and the float-image writes. For those the resolver
their Execute calls was unreachable.

TestSheetSelector_DeferralReachesEveryResolver is that missing tie, and its
counterpart pins that --dry-run keeps the rejection: a preview sends nothing,
so it cannot ask the workbook either, and printing a request whose sheet the
CLI would have filled in would show a call that never existed.

Also asserts the typed envelope in the sheet-prefix conflict E2E case rather
than the message text alone. type / subtype / param are what a caller branches
on; the prose is free to be reworded, and pinning only the prose is what made
that test fail on a reworded message once already.

* style(sheets): drop the redundant loop-variable copies in the deferral test

copyloopvar: `tc := tc` has been unnecessary since Go 1.22, and this module is
on 1.23, so each iteration already gets its own variable. Copied out of habit
from the older tests around it; the parallel subtests behave identically
without it.

* fix(sheets): answer three findings from the second review pass

Quote-aware splitting everywhere. splitRangeAreas used strings.Split while a
quote-aware splitter written in this same branch sat one file away, so
--range "'Q1,Sales'!A1,'Q1,Sales'!B2" was forwarded as FOUR ranges, each half
of a name. rejectMultiAreaRange counted areas the same naive way and would
report four. Both now use splitAreasRespectingQuotes.

The filter commands trade a name for the id they need. filter_id must equal
sheet_id, and neither an omitted selector (the resolver answers with the sole
sheet's NAME) nor an explicit --sheet-name supplies one -- so the old error
told the caller to run +workbook-info and pass it by hand. Execute makes that
trade itself now, dropping the name with it since the two are mutually
exclusive.

The deferral for that lives in the standalone Validate, NOT in the builder.
Relaxing the builder first looked simpler and was wrong: a +batch-update
sub-op is validated through the builder with no execute step of its own, so it
would have shipped a filter op with no filter_id. TestBatchOp_RejectsBadSubOpInput
caught it, and is the guard that keeps it caught.

The omitted-selector lookup declares the read scope it uses. It calls
get_workbook_structure -- a READ -- from commands that mostly declare only the
write scope, so a least-privilege token passed pre-flight and then 403'd inside
the lookup. resolveOmittedSheetSelector now checks the scope before asking, and
the declaration is derived from each shortcut's own flags at registration
rather than written per command, so it cannot drift as commands gain or lose a
selector. 51 of 91 shortcuts qualify; +batch-update already declared it by hand
and is left as it was.

Not addressed here: the [P1] that an explicitly bounded --range should not be
widened to the payload. That is the same open thread two reviewers have now
raised, and it reverses a behaviour that was asked for deliberately, so it
stays a decision rather than a fix.

* fix(sheets): derive the write extent from a bare anchor only, never past a stated rectangle

Two reviewers raised the same [P1]: --range A1:A1 with a 1x2 payload wrote
A1:B1, onto a cell the call never named, with overwrite on by default. The
warning was returned after the write, so it recorded the overreach instead of
preventing it.

The two spellings are now read as the two different things they are:

  - A bare top-left ("A1", or --start-cell) states no extent. It is an anchor,
    the payload supplies the extent, and that is how --csv-put and every
    library these callers arrive from already read it. Unchanged.
  - A rectangle ("A1:B2", and "A1:A1" -- the caller wrote the end cell) states
    a boundary. A payload that fits inside still narrows, which touches
    nothing outside it; a payload that does not fit is refused.

The refusal names both ways to say what was meant: the rectangle that would
hold the payload, and the anchor spelling that takes its extent from --cells.

The distinction is the parsed `anchored` flag, not the presence of a colon, so
a qualified anchor ("Sheet1!A1") keeps anchor semantics instead of falling
into the rectangle branch.

* fix(sheets): budget the table rectangle before padding materializes it

fitColumnsToRows called padShortRows during normalize, while checkCellBudget
runs at the end of validate -- so the cap could only reject a payload the
process had already allocated. One 8,000-cell row followed by 2,000 empty ones
is 54KB of JSON and a 16M-slot matrix: measured 575MB peak RSS against 34MB for
a trivial payload, and larger shapes OOM.

The rectangle is now budgeted before either padding path builds it. Measuring
is cheap because the trim above only reslices, so rows x widest-column-count is
known without allocating anything. Same input now peaks at 34.9MB, level with
the baseline, and a legitimate 250k-cell write is unaffected.

The total accumulates across sheets, so the cap bounds the payload rather than
each sheet alone, and the refusal lands on the sheet that crosses it rather
than after every sheet has padded. Both shapes that reach a padding path are
covered: no columns declared, and a declared list that gets widened.

* fix(sheets): stop resolving a selector whose absence is the contract, and correct the --cells help

Three findings from the review of the last two commits, all regressions this
branch introduced.

+pivot-create's omitted target was being answered by the omitted-selector
resolver. Omitting --target-sheet-* is not a missing selector there -- it tells
the BACKEND to create a fresh sub-sheet, which is the zero-overwrite path the
command's own tips recommend. Resolving it filled in the sole sheet, the one
holding the source data, so the pivot landed on top of it (the tips describe
exactly that outcome: overwritten data and a #REF! anchor); in a multi-sheet
workbook it demanded a selector the command does not require. Both reproduced
against the execute path, which is where this broke -- the existing tests only
covered dry-run and the input builder, neither of which reaches the resolver.

The filter id lookup now checks the read scope too. EnsureScopes was added to
resolveOmittedSheetSelector, but an explicit --sheet-name makes that resolver
return before its own check, and resolveFilterSheetID then issues
get_workbook_structure regardless. Declaring a conditional scope does not
enforce it, so a least-privilege token still reached a 403 from inside the
lookup.

--cells help no longer describes the removed behaviour. It still said an array
larger than --range writes past it, which the previous commit made false; an
agent reading that would construct a request that now cannot succeed.

The canonical spec carries the same stale sentence in three more places, but
that repo is mid-merge with unresolved conflicts in the very file, so this
corrects the CLI-side data/flag-defs.json (regenerating flag_defs_gen.go) and
the shipped skill prose. The canonical edit still has to follow, or the next
sync will reintroduce the old wording.

* fix(sheets): close the two gaps a self-review found in this branch's own work

Audited this branch against the bug classes the reviews kept surfacing --
a behaviour wired into one entry point but not its siblings, and allocation
before the budget that bounds it. Two of my own changes were incomplete.

The table cell budget covered one padding path, not both. The previous commit
guarded fitColumnsToRows, which pads to the WIDEST ROW; normalize pads to the
DECLARED COLUMN COUNT earlier and was untouched, so 8,000 declared columns
against 2,000 one-cell rows still built a 16M-cell rectangle from 80KB of JSON
before checkCellBudget could refuse it. Measured 416MB peak, now 37MB, with
the ragged shape still at 35MB and a legitimate 250k-cell write unaffected.

The structure-read scope covered two call sites, not three. +styles-put closes
a whole-column cell_styles range against the sheet's real grid -- a READ this
branch introduced (b710f901) on a command declaring only the write scope. It
carries no sheet selector, so the flag-derived declaration in Shortcuts()
skips it; it now checks the scope at the read and declares it explicitly.

Also checked and found sound, so recording it rather than re-deriving later:
every alias and reshaping this branch added reaches +batch-update sub-ops
(commandFlagAliases feeds the cobra path, the sub-op dispatcher and the map
flag view alike) and --writes items, with errors attributed to the right item;
padRaggedCellRows already budgets before padding; Shortcuts() stays idempotent
across repeated calls; and no shipped skill text still describes the multi-area
or filter-selector behaviour as it was before this branch changed it.

* fix(sheets): drop two ambiguities a full read of this branch's diff found

Read the whole production diff rather than waiting for the next review round.
Two of my own changes were wrong in ways the tests did not catch.

"above" / "below" were added as compare_type spellings of greaterThan /
lessThan. They should not have been: aboveAverage is a rule_type in the very
same schema, so a caller writing "above" may mean that rule rather than a
comparison. That is exactly the ambiguity the silent-alias bar exists to
refuse, and I did not check the enum before adding them. Removed; "greater" /
"less" stay, since no rule type collides with those.

Lifting border_styles out of cell_styles left an empty cell_styles behind when
the border was its only key, putting a field on the wire that the correctly
spelled payload does not carry. The earlier "byte-identical" check that missed
this was run against +styles-put, a different function; the +cells-set path is
now compared directly and pinned.

This commit also carries an incoming skill sync that landed in the working
tree (SKILL.md, batch-update, formula-translation, formula-verify, and the
--ai-only description), which is not mine. Worth recording because that sync
REVERTED both of the doc fixes from 742b9941 -- the --cells help and the three
write-cells prose spots -- exactly as predicted when they were made. They are
re-applied here on top of the synced text, and they will keep needing that
until the canonical spec carries them; that repo is still mid-merge with the
relevant file conflicted.

* fix(sheets): count the header row in the budget, and refuse a payload wider than the grid

Both reproduced before fixing, both in the table payload path.

The cell budget counted len(Rows) * len(Columns), so a header-only payload was
free: Header=true, zero data rows and 1,000,001 columns gave a product of zero,
sailed past every check this branch added, and buildSheetMatrix then built a
million cell maps for the header alone (measured 809MB peak). All four budget
sites now use one basis -- data rows plus the header row that is actually
materialized. 809MB -> 262MB, the remainder being the 10.8MB of JSON itself,
which has to be parsed before any budget can look at it.

TestTablePutCellBudgetCap caught the consequence and was right to: a 1000x1000
payload really does materialize 1,001,000 cells once the header is counted, so
its fixture now states 999 data rows for a 1,000,000-cell total, and it gained
the header-only case that motivated this.

Separately, the column count a payload ends up with is not always the one it
declared: fitColumnsToRows widens it to the widest data row, so one declared
column and a 201-value row becomes 201 columns. sheetCreateDims clamps a new
grid to 200, making that write a guaranteed API failure -- and on
+workbook-create it fails after the workbook exists, leaving one created but
not written. Refused locally now, counting the anchor offset exactly as
sheetCreateDims does when it sizes the grid.

* fix(sheets): make the AI-formula completion contract say one thing

Four places stated it and no two agreed: the flag help required
ai_formula_total == expected count, the skill said that comparison is invalid,
the command description and the code comment said to poll until pending
clears, and the skill said to deliver with pending and not poll. An agent
could read the same response and reach opposite decisions.

Settled it against a real workbook rather than picking a side. Eight
=AI(...) formulas written into three non-adjacent ranges, all eight confirmed
by read-back to have landed as AI formulas and be computing: --ai-only
reported ai_formula_total = 1 throughout, and pointing --range at the 2-cell
range, the 3-cell range, or a range holding no AI formulas at all returned
byte-identical summaries. So total is neither a count of the cells written nor
narrowed by --range, and the flag help's criterion was unreachable -- eight
formulas can never make it equal eight.

The criterion is now ai_formula_failed_count == 0 everywhere, which is what
the skill already said, with pending formulas delivered and reported rather
than waited on. The description and the comment drop "poll", and the comment
records why total cannot substitute for it. The canonical spec carries the
same two corrections (sheet-skill-spec 88d9ae2a), so this survives the next
sync instead of being reverted by it -- which is what happened twice to the
--cells wording, also fixed at the source now and pulled back in here.

* fix(sheets): finish the grid ceiling at rows, and count the header append forces

The column ceiling landed without its row half. A 50,001-row payload passed
validate(), and the write goes out in batches -- so it lands its first 50,000
rows and fails on the last one. Refused locally now, counting the anchor row
and the header exactly as sheetCreateDims does when it sizes the grid.

append is the case validate() cannot settle: its bottom row depends on what
the sheet already holds. checkAppendRowCeiling runs once lastDataRow comes
back and before the first batch leaves, so an over-long append is refused
whole rather than part-applied.

budgetRows used headerOn, which reports false for append with no explicit
header choice -- but writeSheetData FORCES a header there once it sees the
sheet is empty, so a 5,000x200 append was budgeted at 1,000,000 cells and
materialized 1,000,200. sheetCreateDims already had the correct predicate
inline; it is now one function both call, so the two cannot drift again.

Also carries the skill wording this contract needed: the first-screen rule
said "抽检" (sample) and the reference table said "轮询异步状态" (poll), both
against the criterion the same document already states. Fixed at the canonical
source (sheet-skill-spec 48fbe576) and synced here. The "禁止用 +cells-get
轮询计算结果" line stays -- that one forbids something else and was correct.

* fix(sheets): re-check the grid ceiling against the footprint the styles produce

checkSheetGridCeiling only sees the data matrix, and the styles pass runs
after it. A 1x1 payload with a cell_styles range of A50001 grew the matrix to
50,001 rows, and GS1 grew it to 201 columns -- both past a grid sheetCreateDims
has already clamped, so the write fails remotely with its earlier batches
already applied. cell_merges, row_sizes and col_sizes reach the same way.

Re-checked against workbookCreateStyleDimensions, which is the extent
sheetCreateDims already sizes the grid from -- so the independent visual ops
are covered by the same helper rather than a second rule, and the two cannot
disagree about what the footprint is. append skips the row half, whose base
row is only known remotely; checkAppendRowCeiling still settles that side.

Also carries the reference wording this contract needed. SKILL.md already said
"整个写入区间做一次检查", but four references still called the rule
"异步抽检规则" while formula-verify's own body says "不要抽样" -- the name
contradicted the rule. Nine of them renamed at the canonical source
(sheet-skill-spec 6f76bd7d) and synced here. The one line that uses 抽检 to
describe what it FORBIDS ("子集抽检会漏掉…") is deliberately left alone.

* fix(sheets): stop refusing a payload for a grid ceiling the backend does not have

checkSheetGridCeiling / checkGridCeilingWithStyles / checkAppendRowCeiling read
200 columns and 50000 rows as hard grid ceilings and refused offline. They are
the maxima the CREATE call accepts (+sheet-create validates the same pair), not
a limit on what a sheet may hold, and createSheet's own live-verified note two
functions above already said the backend expands the grid on write.

Probed against a real workbook rather than the message text, 2026-09-14:

  - GS1 (column 201) and IZ1 (column 260) written into a 200-column sheet both
    landed and read back; the grid grew from A1:GR200 to A1:IZ200.
  - A50001 and A60000 on a 20-column sheet landed the same way.
  - The one refusal the backend does issue counts CELLS, not rows or columns:
    "exceeded the maximum number of cells per sheet" (602133003), at 50001x260.

So the quantity worth guarding is the cell count, which checkCellBudgetWithStyles
already bounds at maxTablePutCells, a million cells below the shape that failed
live. What the three checks added was a false rejection of every wide or tall
payload under that budget -- a 260-column table is 260K cells, well inside the
budget and refused before it left. They go; sheetCreateDims keeps the same two
numbers as create-call clamps, with the probe recorded where they are applied.

* fix(sheets): correct three aliases this branch's own review found

wrapBareListValue split a bare --ranges on every comma, so
--ranges "'Q1,Sales'!A1:B2" arrived as two ranges, "'Q1" and "Sales'!A1:B2".
The comment claimed an A1 range never carries a comma, which a quoted sheet
name does; splitAreasRespectingQuotes is the splitter the read expansion was
already moved to in this branch, and it settles this one too.

--outdir / --output-dir went in as domain aliases for --output-path, but the
directory reading is +workbook-export's alone (directoryValuedExportAliases
keeps it from being split into dir+name). Every other --output-path is strictly
a file path, so "+csv-get --outdir ./exports" wrote a file named "exports".
They stay per-command, where +workbook-export already lists them.

+dim-freeze's frozen-* moved from a prescription to a silent rename on the
grounds that the value is the same integer. It is, but the call is not: the
command states the whole freeze state every time, so --frozen-rows 2 alone
ships freeze_rows:2 with no freeze_columns and unfreezes an existing column
freeze the caller never mentioned. Back on the prescription tier, which is
what can name the other axis; the 09-01..08 *-count spellings join it there.</pre>

fix(docx): dump /numbering replays safely into a target that already has lists

A `dump /numbering` rebuilt the source's list definitions as typed adds
addressed by SOURCE position (`/numbering/abstractNum[1]`) and carrying the
source ids (abstractNumId=0, numId=1). Replayed into a document that already
has numbering — the cross-document paragraph-cloning flow behind #404 — the
positional path resolved to the TARGET's own first definition, so the source
levels were appended into it (a bullet list turned decimal), and the
duplicated ids left the file invalid while the cloned paragraph silently
joined the target's unrelated list.

- The emitter now addresses the definition just added via `[last()]`,
  mirroring the `/body/p[last()]` convention.
- `BatchCompat.RemapNumberingIds`, run from the shared `ApplyBatchItems`
  entry (CLI, resident and SDK executor), gives every `w:abstractNum` /
  `w:num` whose id the target (or an earlier item of the batch) already
  uses the next free id and rewrites this batch's references to it: the
  num→abstractNum link and each add/set `numId` prop. Ids the batch does
  not define are left alone — they name the target's own lists.
- `WordHandler.GetNumberingDefinitionIds` exposes the ids currently defined.

Blank targets and self round-trips are unchanged (no collision, no remap;
`last()` equals the sequential position). Verified with tools/rt-ssim.py on
numbering-heavy samples: identical numbering ids/structure, SSIM ≥ 0.9995.
Numbering and paragraph dumps must be replayed in the same batch for the
remap to cover the paragraph's numId.

Refs #404.

fix(docx): raw-set no longer rewrites every w:ind to the ISO-strict spelling

A raw-set that modified /document re-serialized the part through the SDK's
InnerXml setter, which brings every  back as w:start/w:end even when
the source used w:left/w:right — so touching one node rewrote the indent
spelling of every paragraph in the part. A later `set` wrote w:left next to
the now-strict w:start, the element carried two conflicting indents, and a
Word save dropped one side.

Fold the strict aliases back into the transitional spelling right after the
InnerXml round-trip, so the part keeps the spelling it arrived with. The
indent setters now fold BOTH sides through the same helper instead of
clearing only the side being written, so `set indent=` on a strict source no
longer leaves a lone w:end="0" behind.

`officecli help docx move` treated "move" as a schema element and failed
with "unknown element 'move' — did you mean ole?" on stderr and nothing on
stdout, so a caller forwarding help verbatim showed an empty reference.
move/swap/validate/… are commands, not elements, and have no schema page.

When the trailing token names a CLI command, print that command's SCL help
(the same text `officecli move --help` prints) behind a one-line note, and
keep the unknown-element error for tokens that are neither.

Also spell out `move --index` semantics in its help: the element is
detached first and the index applies to the remaining siblings, so moving
p[1] to index 2 in [P1,P2,P3,P4] yields [P2,P3,P1,P4]. The two readings
only differ for backward moves, which is why it went unnoticed.

description:
fix(bridge): block hostile web pages (CSRF, DNS rebinding, WS hijack); add heartbeat

A web page in the user's browser could drive the localhost bridge:

- Blind cross-origin POSTs executed even though CORS hid the response
  (verified: a text/plain POST /compose {send:true} from
  Origin: https://evil.example reached the extension).
- DNS rebinding let a hostile domain read responses same-origin.
- Any page could open ws://127.0.0.1:7701 and replace the extension
  socket, receiving every CLI request and answering with forged data.

The bridge now rejects HTTP requests with an Origin outside
TB_BRIDGE_CORS_ORIGINS, Host headers that are not an IP literal,
localhost, *.localhost, *.internal (host.docker.internal) or listed in
TB_BRIDGE_ALLOWED_HOSTS, and WebSocket handshakes from http(s)/file/null
origins. tb, tb-mcp and curl send no Origin header and are unaffected;
the extension connects from moz-extension://.

The CORS allowlist and WebSocket ping/pong heartbeat (drops sockets that
stop answering, e.g. after sleep) come from PR #20.

fail against the previous bridge.

description:
Enforce TB_AUTH_TOKEN on the bridge HTTP listener

The bridge binds to 127.0.0.1, which prevents remote access but is not
access control: every process running as the same OS user can call it and
read the whole mailbox, whether or not it was wired up to the CLI.

SPEC.md already documented TB_AUTH_TOKEN and both clients already send it
as `Authorization: Bearer `. The daemon never checked it, so the
roadmap item "Auth token support (bridge + CLI)" was only half done.

The bridge now compares the header against TB_AUTH_TOKEN in constant time
and answers 401 when it is missing or wrong. Behaviour is unchanged when
the variable is unset, so the default zero-config setup still works.

Two deliberate choices:

- An empty TB_AUTH_TOKEN aborts startup rather than disabling auth.
  Failing open would leave the bridge unauthenticated with nothing in the
  log to say so.
- The startup banner reports whether auth is enabled, so the state of the
  control is visible without probing for it.

The 401 body carries code AUTH_REQUIRED because clients map an
unrecognised 4xx to THUNDERBIRD_ERROR, which would misreport a missing
token as a Thunderbird fault.

Scope is the HTTP listener only. The WebSocket listener on :7701 that the
extension connects to still accepts any local connection; closing that
needs a change on the extension side and is left for separate work.

Tests spawn the real bridge process rather than a mock.

description:
fix: publish the release from the commit that contains the version (#719)

* fix: publish the release from the commit that contains the version

Mirrors twilio/twilio-cli-core for the same defect. Releases were published
before main was updated, so the git tag and the npm provenance attestation
pointed at a commit that did not contain the version being published. This was
correct before @semantic-release/git was dropped, because that plugin committed
the bump during prepare, ahead of the tag.

The branch ruleset means that commit cannot be pushed during a release, so the
order is inverted instead: decide the version first, land it via PR, then
publish from the merge commit.

  release.yml / release-on-prep-merge.yml -> release-prepare.yml
      semantic-release --dry-run decides the version; prepare-release.js writes
      it into package.json, package-lock.json and CHANGES.md; the result goes
      up as a release PR. Nothing is published.

  release-on-bump-merge.yml -> release-publish.yml (was release-core.yml)
      Runs on the merge commit, which already contains the version, so
      semantic-release tags and publishes a commit that matches what it claims.
      The "propose release commit as a PR" step is gone: the release PR is now
      that commit.

The dry run is load-bearing: semantic-release creates and pushes the tag itself
before the publish plugins run, so a real run during prepare would recreate the
bug it is meant to fix.

verify-release-version.js guards the gap between the two stages, failing the
release if anything merged to main after the release PR was opened and changed
the computed version.

@semantic-release/changelog is dropped, since prepare-release.js writes
CHANGES.md before the tag exists; leaving it in would prepend the same notes a
second time, into the published tarball.

change-log and cli-core-tag are no longer passed into the publish stage, since
the dispatch inputs are gone by then. release-inputs-for-publish.sh recovers
both from the release-prep commit and package.json.

Approval count is unchanged: the prep PR and the release PR, the same two as
before. The release PR now merges before the publish rather than after.

description:
ZulipChat MCP 0.7.3 is a stable bug-fix and security release that completes the transition to MCP 2026-07-28. It uses FastMCP 4.0.4 and MCP SDK/types 2.2.0, preserves legacy-client support, and retains 20 core tools, 60 extended tools, and opt-in background tasks.

The two audit passes addressed credential and cache isolation, owner/request-bound approvals, shell quoting, command-expression execution, HTTP authentication and file boundaries, listener persistence and shutdown, async responsiveness, search ordering and time windows, pagination, workflow rollback, scheduling, and installer output.

Upgrade

uvx --refresh-package zulipchat-mcp zulipchat-mcp --version

Restart your MCP client/server after updating. For a persistent installation, use your package manager to upgrade to zulipchat-mcp==0.7.3.

Behavior changes to review

  • Approvals must name their request: /approve REQUEST_ID or /deny REQUEST_ID. Bare approvals no longer select a pending request implicitly.
  • A selected zuliprc file supplies its email, key, and site together, ahead of ambient credential variables. Restart after changing credential files.
  • Public HTTP binds require a bearer token. Configure --allowed-host for a public hostname. HTTP rejects local filesystem paths, event callbacks, and process-wide identity switching; those local capabilities remain available over stdio.
  • SDK automatic retries of ambiguous failed writes are disabled. Check whether Zulip accepted a send before retrying it.
  • Use search_messages for time filters. Timestamp narrow helpers now reject unsupported filters explicitly. Some date-anchor queries require Zulip 12 / feature level 445.
  • Server-side analytics use ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, with structured-data fallback when no provider is configured. Sampling is deprecated in the new MCP specification. Modern MCP omits ping; legacy ping remains covered.
  • Use a single instance per trusted account for persisted agent sessions, approvals, listener cursors, and task state.

Verification and acknowledgments

The audit suite passes 711 tests with three opt-in live tests skipped, reaching 70.69% branch-aware coverage. Source and clean-wheel smoke tests cover both protocol eras and both tool tiers. See the full changelog and audit report for findings, evidence, and limits.

Thanks to @aurelien-eveil for the native drafts contribution (#15) and @lloydhazlett for the listener timeout contribution (#14). Both are preserved in this release, together with the previously unpublished beta.1 fixes. This release resolves migration trackers #17 and #18.

The generated changes since stable v0.7.2 follow below.
